props.title: Thomasine & Bushrod

sections.content: **Thomasine & Bushrod** (1974) stands as a revolutionary Black Western that deliberately subverts the white-dominated genre conventions of its era. Written by and starring Vonetta McGee alongside Max Julien, the film offers a powerful counter-narrative to traditional Westerns like **Bonnie and Clyde** (1967). Set in 1911 Texas, it follows African American outlaws who steal from racist landlords and redistribute wealth to marginalized communities - a radical premise for 1974 that echoes the social consciousness of Blaxploitation while breaking new ground in the Western genre. sections.content: The film's importance extends beyond its plot - it represents a crucial moment in Black cinema's expansion into traditionally white genres. Director Gordon Parks Jr., fresh off directing **Super Fly** (1972), brings a distinctly Black perspective to Western tropes. Like his contemporary Sidney Poitier with **Buck and the Preacher** (1972), Parks Jr. reclaims the American frontier narrative through a Black lens, highlighting historical truths long ignored by Hollywood Westerns.

McGee and Julien's performances shatter stereotypes with complex characterizations rarely afforded to Black actors in Westerns. Their outlaw lovers are neither villains nor simple heroes, but fully realized characters fighting systemic oppression. This nuanced approach influenced later revisionist Westerns like **Posse** (1993) and **Django Unchained** (2012), which similarly centered Black perspectives in the Old West. sections.content: While **Thomasine & Bushrod** (1974) never achieved the widespread recognition of contemporaneous Blaxploitation hits like **Shaft** (1971), its impact on Black cinema cannot be overstated. The film helped establish a template for Black filmmakers to reclaim and reimagine traditionally white genres through a distinctly African American lens. This approach would later influence directors like Charles Burnett with **To Sleep with Anger** (1990) and Mario Van Peebles with **Posse** (1993).
